DELIVERABLE: This is context poisoning, not a missing-instruction problem: find the first turn where the bad 10,000 claim entered (turn 40), truncate the session back to before it, and restart with verified-only sources reloaded.
BOUNDARY: Do not append louder or repeated corrections or pin them to the system prompt; the poisoned turns would stay in context and keep getting self-referenced.
EVIDENCE: Record the rejected claim and its vendor-page provenance, then replay the batch-sizing task from the clean context and confirm it plans for 1,000/min.

DELIVERABLE: Roll the session back to before turn 40 and start a fresh context containing only verified facts such as the 1,000/min limit from official docs, deleting the poisoned turns instead of correcting them.
BOUNDARY: Another capitalised correction layered on top is often ignored while the bad claim remains in history.
EVIDENCE: Note which source introduced the claim at turn 40 and rerun from the clean state to check batch sizes.

DELIVERABLE: The agent is ignoring the correction, so make it stronger: re-append the correction in capitals at the end of the prompt and pin it in the system prompt with an instruction to disregard 10,000.
BOUNDARY: Do not throw away the session because the 30 turns of planning are valuable.
EVIDENCE: Check at turn 80 that the agent uses 1,000/min.

DELIVERABLE: Not a go yet: a needle test is single-fact retrieval and does not show multi-fact reasoning, synthesis or 12-rule instruction following at 300K. Build a benchmark that mirrors the production workload with real tickets and score root-cause accuracy and format compliance at growing context sizes.
BOUNDARY: Do not approve deployment on the needle score alone; 100% needle recall gives false confidence.
EVIDENCE: Add retrieval variants with low question-needle word overlap (NoLiMa style) and distractor tickets, and compare against shorter contexts.

DELIVERABLE: Hold the decision. The planted-sentence test only proves exact retrieval; run a production-like evaluation on our own tickets covering combining facts across tickets and obeying the output rules, at 100K, 200K and 300K.
BOUNDARY: The needle result is not evidence for reasoning or instruction quality.
EVIDENCE: Include needles that paraphrase the question with no literal overlap and add a distractor ticket; deploy only if the task score holds.

DELIVERABLE: Go: 100% recall at 200K, 500K and 900K with every depth tested comfortably covers our 300K tickets, so approve the rollout.
BOUNDARY: Risk is low because recall is perfect.
EVIDENCE: Monitor the first week of production for complaints.

DELIVERABLE: Do not call this degradation from one run. Repeat the fixed eval several times at each context size to get a baseline and variance, and look for a sustained decline tied to context growth.
BOUNDARY: One 6-point drop can be normal run-to-run noise, so compaction and sub-agent work are premature.
EVIDENCE: Also run the rewritten prompt template on a short context to rule out a prompt-quality problem; if it also scores 82% there, the new sections are the cause.

DELIVERABLE: First gather more data: many runs at turn 10 and at 120K to see whether the 82% is noise, and only a sustained drop justifies degradation work.
BOUNDARY: Do not start compaction on a single data point.
EVIDENCE: Compare the old prompt and the new prompt on a small fresh context to separate prompt changes from context length.

DELIVERABLE: Context degradation is likely at 120K tokens, so begin compaction now and split the agent into sub-agents this sprint.
BOUNDARY: Do not wait for more data because the drop is already visible.
EVIDENCE: Re-run the eval after compaction ships.

DELIVERABLE: Do not rely on the model ignoring irrelevant text. Measure first: compare a clean relevant-only baseline with one distractor and then several distractors, set the cutoff from the observed difference, and stop pre-loading 25 chunks.
BOUNDARY: A cutoff of 0.5 picked by feel is unvalidated.
EVIDENCE: Store policy chunks behind a retrieval tool so they enter context just-in-time, and report accuracy per distractor count against the 84% figure.

DELIVERABLE: Test whether distractors hurt: score the clean context, a single irrelevant chunk, and many irrelevant chunks, then choose the threshold from those results. Switch from pre-loading to on-demand fetching via a search tool call.
BOUNDARY: Assuming irrelevant text is harmless is not acceptable.
EVIDENCE: Compare accuracy against the 84% baseline across distractor levels.

DELIVERABLE: Keep pre-loading but raise the similarity cutoff to 0.7 and trim to the top 10 chunks, which is plenty to cut noise.
BOUNDARY: Having extra chunks mostly just costs tokens.
EVIDENCE: Spot check a few answers afterwards.

DELIVERABLE: Move every fetched page out of the repository root into a run-scoped tree such as runs/<run_id>/sources/evidence/raw/ (e.g. runs/2026-11-07-a/sources/evidence/raw/hyp12_page_0412.html), with a one-line index file per run mapping each raw file to its URL, fetch time, and hypothesis id; proposals cite the full run-relative path.
BOUNDARY: Covers where raw evidence is stored and cited; it does not change scoring or drafting, and no raw dumps stay at the repository root any more.
EVIDENCE: Pick three published proposals and trace each cited claim to a raw file under its own run directory; list the repo root and confirm no page_*.html remains.

DELIVERABLE: Create one directory per run (runs/<run_id>/raw/) and save the pages there, keeping the evaluation and the proposal in the same run folder so evidence sits beside what used it; cite proposals by run-relative path, not the bare file name.
BOUNDARY: Root-level artifacts are the problem, so move the existing page files into the run that fetched them where the run is known and flag the rest as unprovenanced.
EVIDENCE: A reviewer picks any proposal and finds its backing pages in the same run folder in under a minute.

DELIVERABLE: Move the pages into a top-level evidence/ directory with content-hash filenames and a manifest.csv that maps each hash to the proposals that cite it.
BOUNDARY: Only storage layout changes; scoring and drafting stay as they are.
EVIDENCE: Check that every proposal citation resolves to a hash in manifest.csv.

DELIVERABLE: Track three numbers before and after the move: (1) the static-versus-dynamic token ratio, i.e. tokens always in the prompt against tokens loaded on demand per task, (2) total tokens per completed task including every file read, and (3) the load usage rate: how often a loaded file is actually used or cited in the answer, so loads that go unused show up as waste, plus task success on the same eval set.
BOUNDARY: This shows token and quality effects on our eval tasks; it does not prove savings on traffic we did not replay.
EVIDENCE: Replay 200 logged tasks under both setups and report prompt tokens, loaded tokens, usage rate per file, and pass rate side by side.

DELIVERABLE: Do not rely on the 11K to 2K drop. Compare the split between prompt tokens that are always present and tokens loaded when needed, before and after, and log every file load so we can compute what share of loaded files are really referenced in the final answer; add total cost per task and accuracy on a fixed set.
BOUNDARY: Measurement only; no change to which documents are loaded.
EVIDENCE: A before/after table per task type with total tokens, load count, share of loads used, and success rate.

DELIVERABLE: Compare average prompt size and monthly token cost before and after the change, plus a satisfaction survey of the people using the agent.
BOUNDARY: Cost figures only, no per-file analysis.
EVIDENCE: Report the 11K to 2K reduction and the lower bill as the proof.

DELIVERABLE: Hand this to memory-systems: customer, staff, and account are entities with relations and validity dates, and the 'as of last March' question needs temporal and semantic retrieval that file-backed notes cannot give. Stop extending grep over notes/*.md.
BOUNDARY: filesystem-context stays in charge of scratch outputs, plans, and handoff files; context-compression and multi-agent-patterns do not address retrieval and are not used here. The markdown notes stay as the raw record feeding the memory layer.
EVIDENCE: Run the 'managed by someone who left, plan as of March' query on a 200-customer sample against both grep and the memory-systems design and compare recall against a hand-labelled answer set.

DELIVERABLE: Grep over files has hit its limit; this needs entity tracking and as-of-date queries, which memory-systems covers, so use that skill and keep the markdown notes alongside it as the underlying source.
BOUNDARY: Not a summarization problem and not a multi-agent problem, so the other two skills are skipped.
EVIDENCE: Test with 20 known questions, including the left-the-company one, and count how many return the right accounts.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the file layout and add a vector index over notes/*.md with embeddings so paraphrases match, plus a customer-alias glob for renamed accounts.
BOUNDARY: Retrieval over existing notes only.
EVIDENCE: Compare top-5 hit rate before and after on 20 sample questions.

DELIVERABLE: Do not adopt the scratch/grep plan: the file-backed pattern assumes the model can run grep and read ranges, and this endpoint has no tool calling or file access, so it would only add I/O latency. Instead cut the pasted lookups in the backend before the call: extract only the fields the answer needs, truncate or summarize each result to a budget, and drop duplicates.
BOUNDARY: This is token-efficiency work that needs no file storage, so context-optimization tactics apply; file offload becomes an option only if the endpoint gains tools.
EVIDENCE: Log prompt tokens and answer quality on 100 logged tickets before and after trimming and confirm the success rate holds.

DELIVERABLE: Not workable as proposed since the model cannot open files or call grep. Let the backend do the selection: filter and rank the lookup results, keep the top relevant parts, and summarize the rest to a fixed size per lookup.
BOUNDARY: Model has no file access, so no scratch directory for it; if tool calling is added later, revisit offloading.
EVIDENCE: Compare tokens per request and resolution accuracy on a sample of past tickets.

DELIVERABLE: Yes, write each lookup result to scratch/lookup_<id>.txt, keep a 100-token summary in the prompt, and add a grep tool so the model pulls the details it needs.
BOUNDARY: Applies to the three lookups only.
EVIDENCE: Measure prompt tokens before and after the change.

DELIVERABLE: No cache until a profiler says so; the lookup is a 60-entry dict read. When it measurably matters: `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` on shipping_zone.
BOUNDARY: Skipped: caching; add when profiling shows shipping_zone on a hot path.
EVIDENCE: Ask for the profile or latency number that motivates it; no check needed for a non-change.

DELIVERABLE: I would not add a cache yet. A dict lookup over about 60 codes already returns in microseconds and nothing has been measured. If a benchmark later shows a problem, use functools.lru_cache rather than a custom class.
BOUNDARY: Skipping the cache for now; revisit once someone measures a real slowdown.
EVIDENCE: The request has no profile or complaint behind it, so there is nothing to verify.

DELIVERABLE: `from functools import lru_cache\n@lru_cache(maxsize=None)\ndef shipping_zone(country_code): return ZONES[country_code]`
BOUNDARY: The input domain is about 60 codes so the cache is bounded.
EVIDENCE: assert shipping_zone('DE') == shipping_zone('DE')

DELIVERABLE: `import time
_c = {}
def get_user_permissions(user_id):
    k = (current_tenant.get(), user_id); hit = _c.get(k)
    if hit and time.monotonic() - hit[0] < 30: return hit[1]
    v = auth.fetch(user_id); _c[k] = (time.monotonic(), v); return v` The key includes the tenant, entries expire after 30 s, and an admin revocation should also pop the key.
BOUNDARY: Skipped: LRU eviction; add when the dict's memory use becomes a problem (cap it at a fixed size then).
EVIDENCE: `assert` that the same user_id under two tenants gives two entries, and that an entry older than 30 s is refetched.

DELIVERABLE: I key the cache on (tenant, user_id) because current_tenant is hidden state, give each entry a 30 second TTL so revocations take effect quickly, and drop the key on revoke. Code: `def get_user_permissions(user_id): key = (current_tenant.get(), user_id); ...` with a small dict storing (expiry, value).
BOUNDARY: A bare lru_cache would leak permissions across tenants and never expire.
EVIDENCE: Check: two tenants with the same user_id must not share an entry; an expired entry must be refetched.

DELIVERABLE: `from functools import lru_cache\n@lru_cache(maxsize=10000)\ndef get_user_permissions(user_id): return auth.fetch(user_id)`
BOUNDARY: Bounded to 10000 entries so memory stays flat.
EVIDENCE: Call it twice with the same id and confirm the auth service is hit once.

DELIVERABLE: `def page_slice(items, page, size): start = (page - 1) * size; return items[start:start + size]\nassert page_slice([1, 2, 3, 4], 1, 2) == [1, 2]`
BOUNDARY: Noticed page_count drops a trailing partial page (total // size); not touched as it was not reported.
EVIDENCE: The assert fails on the old code (returns [3, 4]) and passes now.

DELIVERABLE: Change only the start line in page_slice to `start = (page - 1) * size`. Check: add `def test_first_page(): assert page_slice([1, 2, 3, 4], 1, 2) == [1, 2]`.
BOUNDARY: Separate issue I saw but left alone: page_count uses floor division and undercounts when total is not a multiple of size.
EVIDENCE: Run the test: before the change page 1 returns the second page.

DELIVERABLE: `def page_slice(items, page, size): start = (page - 1) * size; return items[start:start + size]\ndef page_count(total, size): return -(-total // size)`
BOUNDARY: I also fixed page_count since it truncated partial pages.
EVIDENCE: Reasoned through page 1 with size 2; looks right.

DELIVERABLE: Here is the class you asked for: `class TaxRateCache: def __init__(self): self._c = {}  def get(self, region): ...  def clear(self): self._c.clear()`. One alternative to weigh: functools.lru_cache on the function gives the same thing with less code.
BOUNDARY: Implemented as requested; your call whether to switch.
EVIDENCE: Check: get twice returns same value and clear forces a recompute.

DELIVERABLE: Out of scope for security-review: the risk is agent tool authority, since the LLM picks cmd after reading untrusted pages, so this is prompt injection reaching a shell. Route to tool-design for the tool's permissions and to hosted-agents or harness-engineering for the sandbox and credential boundary; no application-level severity rating is issued here.
BOUNDARY: Handed off before tracing sinks; security-review covers application trust boundaries, not agent permission models, and no scanner or tests were run.
EVIDENCE: The snippet shows cmd supplied by the model and run with shell=True, which is the agent-authority boundary the other playbooks own.

DELIVERABLE: I would not use the application security-review lens on this. A web page can steer the model, so the question is what authority the tool grants: send it to tool-design (narrow tool, allowlisted commands) and harness-engineering (sandbox, approvals).
BOUNDARY: This is a routing answer only; nothing was run or scanned.
EVIDENCE: run_command passes a model-chosen string to a shell, and the model reads customer-supplied pages.

DELIVERABLE: SEVERITY: HIGH. app/agent.py run_command passes cmd to subprocess.run with shell=True, so a page that steers the model gets code execution. Fix: use an argument list with shell=False and validate the binary against an allowlist.
BOUNDARY: Reviewed only this function; no tests or scanners were run.
EVIDENCE: The cmd value is attacker-influenced via page content and reaches a shell sink with no validation.

DELIVERABLE: SEVERITY: HIGH. app/catalog.py lookup, db.execute with an f-string. Input: id=0 UNION SELECT email, pw_hash FROM users. html.escape is HTML encoding at the wrong layer; it does not neutralize SQL, and id is unquoted so no quote is needed. Impact: any self-registered account reads other users' data. Fix: db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE id = ?", (req.args["id"],)) as a parameterized query.
BOUNDARY: Reviewed only this handler; no scanner or tests were run, so nothing is claimed clean.
EVIDENCE: Regression check: 
def test_lookup_rejects_injection(client):
    r = client.get('/products/lookup?id=0 OR 1=1')
    assert len(r.json()) == 0
It fails on the current code and passes after parameterization.

DELIVERABLE: This is vulnerable and HIGH: the escape does nothing for SQL, so id=1 OR 1=1 or a UNION SELECT works for any ordinary logged-in user. Use a parameterized query with a placeholder for id.
BOUNDARY: Only this handler was reviewed and nothing was executed.
EVIDENCE: Add a regression test that sends id=1 OR 1=1 and asserts that it returns no extra rows; it must fail before the fix.

DELIVERABLE: SEVERITY: MEDIUM. The id is concatenated into SQL; html.escape is not enough, so cast it with int(pid) before the query and keep the login requirement.
BOUNDARY: Only this handler was reviewed and nothing was run.
EVIDENCE: The f-string places pid directly in the WHERE clause of the SELECT.

DELIVERABLE: No reachable finding. The f-string puts order into ORDER BY, but order is only ever a value from the fixed SORTS dict (unknown sort falls back to newest), so the attacker's sort string never reaches the SQL text; tenant_id is a bound parameter from req.user.
BOUNDARY: Boundaries checked: sort query arg to the execute sink, tenant scoping at the query, no secrets or logging in this code, result size capped by LIMIT 100; no tests or scanners were run.
EVIDENCE: SORTS.get(req.args.get("sort"), SORTS["newest"]) is an allowlist lookup, so a guard upstream of the sink prevents injection; an empty finding list is the result.

DELIVERABLE: This handler is not exploitable: the interpolated order value comes from a fixed dictionary, never from the request string, and the tenant filter is parameterized. I am reporting no findings.
BOUNDARY: I checked the input to SQL path, the tenant isolation, and the response size; nothing was executed.
EVIDENCE: The sort argument is only a lookup key into SORTS, with a default for anything unknown.

DELIVERABLE: LOW: the f-string in ORDER BY is a SQL injection pattern; hardening suggestion is to validate the sort or use a query builder.
BOUNDARY: Reviewed only app/projects.py and nothing was run.
EVIDENCE: The line f"... ORDER BY {order} LIMIT 100" interpolates a value into SQL.

DELIVERABLE: SEVERITY: MEDIUM. app/admin.py audit_search, db.execute with an f-string. Input: actor=' OR '1'='1 or a UNION SELECT, sent by a platform_admin. The injection is real, but the caller must hold the elevated platform_admin role that ops provisions, so it is bounded by that precondition. Fix: db.execute("SELECT ts, action FROM audit_log WHERE actor = ?", (actor,)) as a parameterized query.
BOUNDARY: Role gate checked at the decorator; reach is limited to provisioned admins; no tests or scanners were run.
EVIDENCE: Regression check: \ndef test_actor_injection(admin_client):\n    assert admin_client.get("/admin/audit/search?actor=x' OR '1'='1").json() == []

DELIVERABLE: This is a real SQL injection, rated MEDIUM instead of HIGH since only an ops-provisioned platform admin can reach the endpoint. Switch to a bound parameter for actor.
BOUNDARY: I relied on the stated provisioning of the role and ran nothing.
EVIDENCE: The actor query arg goes straight into the SELECT text inside quotes.

DELIVERABLE: SEVERITY: HIGH. SQL injection in audit_search: actor is concatenated into the query, which allows reading or altering any table. Use a parameterized query.
BOUNDARY: Reviewed only this handler and nothing was run.
EVIDENCE: The f-string embeds actor inside single quotes with no escaping.
